pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Fair testing

- **Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils are taught to use the following practical scientific methods, processes and skills — "setting up simple practical enquiries, comparative and fair tests" and "making systematic and careful observations and, where appropriate, taking accurate measurements using standard units". Fair/comparative testing is one of the five named enquiry types (observing over time; pattern seeking; identifying/classifying/grouping; comparative and fair testing; researching secondary sources) — it should be named honestly, not defaulted to.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 Planning & Carrying Out Investigations):** the K–2 progression is "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-2, 1-PS4-1, 1-PS4-3, 2-LS2-1, 2-LS4-1, 2-PS1-1, K-PS2-1, K-PS3-1]"; the 3–5 progression sharpens this to "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4]." This topic (ages 7–9) sits on that K–2→ 3–5 boundary: fair tests are introduced and the control-one-variable idea is made explicit.

- **Operational details:** Builds on the KS1 root of performing simple tests (prerequisite mt_Wa44s-f8Ws). The core move is the three-variable analysis of any comparative test: the variable you CHANGE (independent), the variable you MEASURE (dependent), and the variables you KEEP THE SAME (controls) — taught at this age in child language ('change one thing, measure one thing, keep everything else the same'). A test is 'fair' precisely because only one thing changed, so any difference in the result can be attributed to that one change. Feeds forward to controlling variables and independent enquiry planning (dependents mt_ArVBEpMAPk, mt_7VrR1GzhrN).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). A learner who can explain what makes a test fair (one variable changes, the rest stay the same), identify the change/measure/keep-same variables in a given test, and set up a simple comparative or fair test with support has met the bar. Formal independent/dependent variable vocabulary and full independent planning are later tiers (mt_ArVBEpMAPk, mt_Ae56umVlTT).
bestPractices: Teach the three-variable frame in child language on a concrete example first — 'change one thing (the ramp surface), measure one thing (how far the car rolls), keep everything else the same (same car, same height, same push)' — before ever using the words independent/dependent/control.

Make UNFAIRNESS the teaching engine: show a rigged test where two things were changed at once (rougher surface AND steeper ramp) so pupils feel that you genuinely cannot tell which change caused the result — this builds the necessity of controlling variables far better than being told the rule.

Name the enquiry type honestly and don't over-default to fair testing — the AKSIS research shows fair tests dominate over half of primary practicals at the expense of pattern-seeking, observing over time, classifying and research; help pupils recognise WHEN a fair test is the right tool versus another enquiry type.
Use predict-then-test: pupils commit to a prediction before running the comparative test, so the result is something to check against an idea, not just an activity.
Keep the number of variables tiny and the apparatus familiar (ramps, plants, materials, dissolving) so cognitive load is on the fair-test reasoning, not on unfamiliar equipment.
keyRepresentations: The change / measure / keep-the-same three-column planner (the age-appropriate precursor to independent / dependent / control)
A side-by-side comparative set-up (e.g. two ramps, two cups, two plants) where exactly one condition differs
A 'spot the unfair test' contrast pair — one where two things changed, one where only one changed
A simple results table with the changed variable in one column and the measured outcome in the next
A predict → test → compare loop card
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a 'fair test' means being nice/taking turns (the everyday meaning of 'fair') rather than a controlled comparison where only one variable changes.
Changing more than one variable at a time and still believing the result is trustworthy — not seeing that you then can't attribute the effect to any single cause.
Believing every scientific question needs a fair test — over-applying it to questions better answered by observing over time, pattern-seeking or research (the AKSIS over-default).
Confusing the variable you change with the variable you measure (mixing up the input and the outcome).
Forgetting the 'keep the same' variables entirely — controlling only the obvious ones and leaving hidden variables uncontrolled.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach fair/comparative testing through the child-language three-variable frame — change one thing, measure one thing, keep everything else the same — anchored in concrete apparatus (ramps and cars, paper planes, plants, dissolving). Build the necessity of controlling variables by letting an unfair test (two things changed at once) become genuinely uninterpretable, so pupils feel why isolation matters rather than only being told. Complement design practice with recognition tasks (spot-the-unfair-test, sort factors into change/measure/keep-same) and justification dialogue, and honestly name when a fair test is the right enquiry type versus observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying, or research.

activities.title: Design the ramp race: isolate one variable
feedback: If two variables differ between the runs, respond: 'Two things changed — we can't tell which one caused the difference. Which of your two set-ups differs in more than one way?' Have the child rebuild so only one variable changes.

When exactly one variable differs and the rest match, confirm: 'Only the surface changed — that's what makes it fair. Run it again: if the difference in distance keeps showing up, we can put it down to the surface.'
If the child muddles the input and outcome ('I'll measure the surface'), sort the factors into the three-column frame before running.
activities.rationale: Fair testing is a design skill: the child actively chooses what to change, measure, and hold constant and then sees the consequence. Letting an unfair comparison fail to yield an interpretable answer makes the one-variable rule felt. An interactive bench that greys out the result when two variables change (with 'Hmm — two things changed, so we can't tell which caused this') is one concrete way to deliver the insight, not the only medium; the same reasoning can be run with real ramps, a car and a tape measure. NGSS's 3–5 emphasis on controlling variables and considering the number of trials matches the intended insight here.
sourceClaims: DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to be taught to set up simple practical enquiries, comparative and fair tests, as one of the named enquiry types.
NGSS SEP 3 progresses from K-2 'simple investigations based on fair tests' to 3-5 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4]'.
learnerActions: Set up two ramps and a toy car. For each ramp choose values for the conditions: surface (smooth/rough), height, and starting push.
Choose what to measure — e.g. how far the car rolls.
First deliberately make ramp B BOTH rougher AND steeper than ramp A, run both, and try to say which change caused the difference in distance.
Notice you cannot attribute the result to one cause; then rebuild so only ONE condition (e.g. the surface) differs and everything else is identical, and run it again.
Run each set-up more than once and check the result is consistent before concluding.
As you configure, fill in a 'change / measure / keep-the-same' tray recording which variable you changed, which you measured, and which you held constant.
activities.intendedInsight: A test is fair because only one thing changed, so a difference in the result that shows up again when you repeat the runs can be put down to that single change; when two things change at once the result cannot tell you which cause produced it.

activities.title: Paper-plane fair test: build it and throw it
feedback: If the big-wing plane is made from thicker card or paper too, or thrown harder: 'Your two planes differ in more than one way, so a difference in distance can't be pinned on the wings. Rebuild so only the wings change.'
If throws drift (different spots or throwers) without the child noticing: 'Name each thing that must stay the same and why it would otherwise affect how far the plane flies.'
If the plan muddles roles ('I'll change the distance'): sort into change / measure / keep-the-same before starting.
activities.rationale: This activity is exactly the DfE requirement to set up and carry out a comparative/fair test. Genuine set-up — not recitation — reveals real understanding: a child can recite 'change one thing' yet build a confounded test (this production-vs-recitation and predict-then-test framing is pedagogy, not a specific source finding). Predict-then-test makes the result something to check against an idea, and familiar apparatus keeps cognitive load on the fair-test reasoning.
sourceClaims: DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to be taught to set up simple practical enquiries, comparative and fair tests, as one of the named enquiry types.
learnerActions: Question: do paper aeroplanes fly further with bigger wings? Using paper and a tape measure, set up a fair test to answer it.
Before throwing, state what you will change (wing size), what you will measure (how far each plane flies), and what you will keep the same (same paper, same throwing spot, same thrower, same effort).
Make a prediction, then throw both planes a couple of times, holding the one-variable rule as you go.
Record each throw's distance in a simple two-column results table (changed variable | measured distance).
Compare the results against your prediction and say which variable was changed, which measured, and which kept the same.
activities.intendedInsight: Setting up and carrying out a real comparative test requires deliberately holding hidden conditions constant; what you DON'T hold the same (different paper, a harder throw for one plane, a different thrower) is what breaks fairness.

activities.title: Spot the unfair test and sort the variables
feedback: For a wrong 'fair' judgement, point to the second changed variable: 'Two things differ here, so you couldn't tell which caused the result.'
If a question is forced into a fair test when it suits observing over time (e.g. 'how does the plant change over weeks?'), name the better-fitting enquiry type and why.
Confirm correct role sorting by linking each column to the reasoning: the kept-the-same column is what lets us link the result to the one thing we changed (and repeating the test helps check it).
activities.rationale: These recognition and matching tasks assess the evidence statements reliably but mainly check recognition; they consolidate rather than build the design intuition, so they should pair with the hands-on set-up tasks rather than replace them. Honest naming of enquiry type counters the tendency to over-apply fair testing.
sourceClaims: Primary practicals over-default to fair testing (over half) at the expense of other enquiry types such as pattern-seeking and observing over time.
learnerActions: Look at a contrast pair of set-ups: one where two things changed and one where only one changed. Decide which is fair and explain why.
For a given test, sort its factors into three columns: what is changed, what is measured, what is kept the same.
Match investigation questions to the right enquiry type — fair test, observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying/grouping, or researching — and say why a fair test is or isn't the best tool.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising fairness and correctly assigning variable roles reinforces the frame; not every question needs a fair test — some are better answered by observing over time, pattern-seeking, or research.

activities.title: Justify your plan with a science partner
feedback: If the child can't say why a condition matters, ask how that condition would otherwise affect the measured outcome.
If a hidden variable is uncontrolled, prompt: 'Is there anything else different between your two set-ups that we haven't talked about?'
activities.rationale: Socratic dialogue probes justification and surfaces hidden variables, useful after a hands-on test; a conversation alone cannot run the test or show the uninterpretable result, so it supplements the design work rather than replacing it.
learnerActions: Explain your planned test aloud to a partner or in-role scientist.

Answer probing questions: Why keep the ramp height (or throwing spot) the same? What is the one thing you're changing, and what are you measuring? Name two things you're keeping the same and why they matter.
Hunt for hidden uncontrolled variables you may have missed and adjust your plan.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify WHY each condition is held constant — not just list them — shows the reasoning behind fairness and surfaces hidden variables.

constraints: This topic sits on the K–2 → 3–5 boundary: fair tests are introduced and the control-one-variable idea made explicit. Teach the three-variable frame in child language first; formal independent/dependent/control vocabulary and full independent planning are later stages.

Builds on the prerequisite of performing simple tests (KS1). The checkpoint is met when a learner can explain what makes a test fair, identify the change/measure/keep-same variables in a given test, and set up a simple comparative/fair test with support.

Recognition and matching tasks (spot-the-unfair-test, sorting factors) can teach and check classification but do not by themselves elicit the independent design of a controlled comparison; include genuine set-up tasks.

A labelled static set-up with tap-to-reveal can serve as a reference aid naming the parts of a fair test, but a fixed picture cannot recompute, so it cannot deliver the 'two things changed' consequence on its own; use it to support, not as the main teach.
Keep the number of variables small and apparatus familiar so cognitive load stays on fair-test reasoning, not unfamiliar equipment.
Don't over-default to fair testing: help pupils recognise when another enquiry type (observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying, research) fits the question better.
Watch out for the everyday meaning of 'fair' (being nice / taking turns); clarify the scientific meaning of a controlled comparison where only one variable changes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels its interactive-bench rationale with 'no static medium can do' and '3D adds nothing' style comparative-necessity claims; these are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped proposals (an interactive bench is one concrete route to the insight, equivalent to real apparatus). The grey-out panel and settable-condition examples are preserved as optional interaction mechanisms, not mandatory ones.

The production-vs-recitation and predict-then-test justifications in the paper-plane activity are pedagogy; the attached DfE claim supports only the curricular content (setting up comparative/fair tests), not those specific efficacy claims.
The AKSIS over-default claim is marked verified:false in the source; it is retained as supporting the 'name the enquiry type honestly' principle, but its evidence strength is unconfirmed.

The ramp and paper-plane apparatus is used only illustratively: changing more than one condition confounds a distance comparison. No specific distances and no directional force/motion outcomes are asserted, so no force/motion idealisation claim is made; keep it that way if the activity is extended.

Feedback was softened from 'the difference must be down to the surface' to 'can be put down to the surface' and a repeat-trial check was added, so a single run is not treated as conclusive — consistent with the cited NGSS number-of-trials element.

probeDeeper: What is the one thing you're changing? What are you measuring?
Name two things you're keeping the same, and why they matter.
If you used thick card for the big-wing plane and thin paper for the small one, would that be fair? How would you know what caused the difference?
Is this a fair test, or would watching something over time fit this question better?
assess.correctAnswer: The child changes only the wing size, measures how far each plane flies, and keeps everything else the same — same paper, same throwing spot, same thrower, same effort. They set it up and throw while holding the one-variable rule, and can name which variable is changed, which measured, and which kept the same.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confounded test: changes more than one variable — makes the big-wing plane from thicker paper too, or throws it harder — so any difference can't be pinned on the wings.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'which of your two planes is different in more than one way?' Rebuild so only the wings change.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The set-up: two planes differ in more than one way, or the throw differs between them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Variable-role confusion: muddles what to change with what to measure — 'I'll change the distance' or 'I'll measure the wings'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort into a three-column frame — what I change / what I measure / what I keep the same — before starting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child's declared plan assigns the wrong role to a variable.

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't hold conditions constant: throws from different spots, or lets different people throw, without seeing the problem.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name each thing that must stay the same and why it would otherwise affect the distance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: During the throws, the keep-the-same conditions drift and the child doesn't flag it.

responseLevels.gap: Sets up a test where several things differ, or muddles which variable to change and which to measure.
responseLevels.full: Sets up a genuinely fair test — one variable changed, one measured, the rest deliberately kept the same — and can say why controlling the others makes the result trustworthy.
responseLevels.partial: Changes one variable and measures an outcome, but forgets to hold some conditions constant, or needs prompting to name the keep-the-same variables.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: We want to find out whether paper aeroplanes fly further with bigger wings. Here's paper and a tape measure. Set up a fair test to answer it — as you get it ready, show me what you'll change, what you'll measure, and what you'll keep the same. Then do a couple of throws. I'll watch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching reveals whether the child genuinely isolates one variable — the give-away is what they DON'T hold constant (different paper, a harder throw for the big-wing plane, different throwers). A child can recite 'change one thing' yet build an unfair test; the set-up, not the recitation, shows real understanding.
